price_per_million.source: copied from reasoning_models_v1 (confirmed 2026-11-11); thinking tokens billed as output

research_concepts: sequence/adjacency of play types within a possession
methodological_questions: Can a teammate drive preceding a PNR be identified reliably from play-by-play and the derived possession records?
Is any PPP difference causal, or is it produced by label construction, survivorship (the possession continues after the drive), player/lineup/opponent confounding, or regression to the mean?
How much do label error and foul leakage distort DRIVE and PNR PPP?
Is there enough drive-then-PNR exposure to detect an effect, and how would a claim about 'any' teammate be tested?

historical_evidence.finding: Play-type label audit overall FAIL: OTHER 20.2% vs <10% target, 40.8% low confidence, DRIVE foul-draw 1.7% vs 14-22% benchmark, most play types' PPP above benchmark band. Recorded failure mechanism: C_artifact. Limits recorded: label error, leakage, small sample.
OTHER PPP inflated by 36% foul endings; DRIVE 12pp below foul benchmark (FOUL_LEAK); PNR shows a 22% foul rate; only 335 of 50,668 possessions (0.7%) map to a real play type via initiation_type.

Play-type label backfill verification final FAIL: PNR 28.7% vs 20-28% band, 3100 games with team PNR >33%, team identity FAIL, 82.8% of PNR labels proxy_calibrated; PNR PPP 0.948 passed. 921,514 possessions.

PBP-derived shot-level PNR share of half-court shots varies by team (OKC 7.567% to IND 13.824% in 2024-25). The rates are a calibration input for PBPProxyPNR; calibrated PNR is about 17.9-19.6% of possessions. No pass/fail gate.

Stability of top suppressors and teammate X->Y sequence premiums: only 2/30 stars stable across seasons (B_powered_null). Includes the descriptive negative premium Giannis->Lillard DRIVE->PNR -0.263 (n=31). Min n=20/cell, limited by small sample.
Star suppression gaps were found without placebo or matching; the record notes later sequence work treated similar star-chain gaps as artifacts. Risk flagged: placebo dependence.
DRIVE PPP RS 1.198 vs PO 0.912 (25 teams, no CIs); PNR -0.173. Shows play-type PPP differs between regular season and playoffs, so pooling them risks context confounding.
Play-type PPP across playoff series buckets (1197 records, no CIs): PNR +0.087, DRIVE +0.060. Observational, with selection/regression-to-the-mean caveats.
On-ball coverage labelling from the matchup/PBP feed failed the gate (14.9% and 3.3% labeled; switches_on unpopulated). Matchup fields are therefore not usable to control for coverage.
Player routing comparison: 0 of 8 divergences scoreable because players were missing from the graph database. Shows sparsity and coverage limits in the graph data.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Inferred play-type labels used as a valid basis for PPP comparisons
failed_approaches.why: Audit FAIL; label error and leakage; foul possessions leak into OTHER; DRIVE foul-draw rate far below benchmark (C_artifact).

failed_approaches.what_framing: PPP differences by derived play type read as real efficiency
failed_approaches.what_failed: PPP differences by derived play type read as real efficiency
failed_approaches.why: Foul-ending share inflates or deflates PPP by play type (FOUL_BUCKET, FOUL_LEAK); initiation_type maps only 0.7% of possessions; artifact found.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Backfilled labels (including proxy-calibrated PNR) as a trusted PNR measure
failed_approaches.why: Final FAIL on shares, team identity and game-level PNR rates; 82.8% of PNR labels proxy_calibrated.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Teammate X->Y sequence premiums as stable effects
failed_approaches.why: Adequately powered null on cross-season stability; cells are small (min n=20) and unstable.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Descriptive star and sequence gaps without placebo or matching
failed_approaches.why: No placebo or matching; later work treated similar gaps as artifacts.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Labelling on-ball defensive coverage from the matchup feed
failed_approaches.why: Low confident-label rates and unpopulated switches_on; coverage cannot be controlled with these fields.

evidence_establishes: As recorded, the derived play-type labels failed audits (FAM:SF-APPM-014, FAM:SF-APPA-030), with foul-ending leakage that distorts DRIVE and OTHER PPP (FAM:SF-CHT-025).
PNR labels are largely proxy-calibrated (82.8%), not directly observed (FAM:SF-APPA-030).
Teammate-sequence premiums (including a negative DRIVE->PNR premium, Giannis->Lillard, n=31) are small-n and not stable across seasons (FAM:SF-APPA-058).
Play-type PPP shifts between regular season and playoffs (FAM:SF-APPS-011), so context must be controlled.
Coverage/defensive-scheme fields could not be labeled at usable rates (FAM:SF-APPS-058).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a teammate drive causally raises or lowers PNR PPP on average. No retrieved record tested this contrast directly.
Whether drive-then-PNR sequences can be identified in the raw PBP with accuracy, since only the derived labels were audited.
Any sample size for drive-then-PNR sequences league-wide. Only star-pair cells (n about 31) were reported.
Whether the audit failures bias the drive-before-PNR contrast in a particular direction.
own_inferences: 'Any teammate DRIVE' is a universal claim. A single credible counterexample, such as the recorded negative Giannis->Lillard premium (descriptive, n=31), would contradict it. A defensible test is of the average effect, with heterogeneity reported separately.

If the derived possession records assign one play type per possession, a drive that precedes a PNR on the same possession may be unrepresentable. Adjacency would then have to be rebuilt from raw PBP event order.

Conditioning on a PNR occurring after a drive selects possessions in which the drive did not end the possession (no shot, no foul, no turnover), so PPP is mechanically biased. Drive possessions that end in fouls or shots are excluded from the 'preceded' group.
Pace, shot-clock time remaining and lineup quality likely differ between drive-first and non-drive-first PNRs. Raw PPP differences would therefore be confounded.
Because DRIVE and PNR labels both come from the same PBP and the same proxy rules, label errors are likely correlated across the two. That could create or hide an association.
uncertainties: Whether raw PBP event types (drive, pass, screen proxies) are fine enough to define a PNR independent of the proxy-calibrated labels.
Real exposure of drive-then-PNR sequences by season and by player.
The form of the 2025-26 playoff data on 2026-06-14, which is partial until 2026-06-21.
Whether the graph database stores event order or only possession-level labels.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history, a straightforward observational comparison of PNR PPP with versus without a preceding drive might have looked acceptable. The retrieved records show failed label audits, foul-leakage artifacts, proxy-calibrated PNR labels and unstable sequence premiums. These moved the decision to do_not_proceed on the derived labels as posed, with a restricted minimum viable test on raw PBP.

blocking_constraints.text: DRIVE and PNR labels failed audits; 82.8% of PNR labels are proxy_calibrated; drive foul-draw rate far below benchmark (FAM:SF-APPM-014, FAM:SF-APPA-030).
Play-type assignment and foul endings depend on possession outcomes, so PPP by label is partly constructed (FAM:SF-CHT-025).
Requiring the possession to continue into a PNR after a drive conditions on survival and excludes drive possessions ending in shots, fouls or turnovers.
Per-teammate or per-pair cells are small (n about 20-31) and unstable; the universal 'any teammate' claim cannot be powered cell by cell.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved record tested whether a teammate drive preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP. Related work shows label audit failures, foul-leakage artifacts, proxy-calibrated PNR labels, unstable teammate-sequence premiums (including one descriptive negative DRIVE->PNR premium) and unusable coverage labels. These bear on feasibility, not on the answer.

risks.text: Derived DRIVE and PNR labels failed audits and PNR is mostly proxy-calibrated, so exposure and outcome are both mismeasured.
Foul-ending and outcome-based label rules make play-type PPP partly a construction artifact.
Conditioning on possession continuation after a drive biases PPP among drive-then-PNR possessions.
Player, lineup, opponent, game-state, shot-clock time and regular season/playoff context drive both the drive-first sequence and PPP; defensive coverage cannot be controlled (FAM:SF-APPS-058).
Small cells for specific teammate pairs; no CIs in prior records.
Drive-then-PNR sequences may be rare per player-season.
Selecting high-PPP players or pairs inflates apparent effects, which then regress.
PNR identification from PBP proxies has uncertain precision and recall.
Testing 'any teammate' across many players or pairs yields spurious positives.
Label rules and play-type PPP differ by season and by regular season vs playoffs.
Prior sequence gaps were reported without placebo or matching and later treated as artifacts.

design.estimand: Average within-team difference in PNR PPP (points per possession, excluding or separately reporting foul-ending possessions) between PNR possessions preceded within the same possession by a teammate drive and otherwise comparable PNRs with no preceding drive, estimated first as a pooled average, then with heterogeneity by player. The universal 'any teammate' reading is treated as falsified if the pooled CI excludes a positive effect or a pre-specified share of adequately powered player strata show a negative effect.
design.unit: Half-court possession containing a PNR identified from raw PBP event order (not from the proxy-calibrated labels), clustered by game and team.
design.sample: 2022-23 through 2024-25 regular seasons and playoffs, plus the complete 2025-26 regular season, with regular season and playoffs analyzed separately. Exclude the 2025-26 playoffs (partial on 2026-06-14, complete 2026-06-21) from the confirmatory test and use them only as an untouched holdout once complete. Exclude garbage time, transition, and possessions with fewer than a minimum number of seconds before the drive-to-PNR hand-off. A hand-labelled audit sample (for example 300 possessions) is needed to measure PNR and drive precision and recall before any analysis.
design.power: Compute before analysis: count drive-then-PNR possessions by season and player and the achievable minimum detectable effect (SD of possession points about 1.1-1.3 and clustering), and require a minimum detectable effect of about 0.05-0.08 PPP at pooled level. Do not test pair-level cells below n=100. Prior cells (n about 20-31) are underpowered. If the pooled minimum detectable effect is too large, or labelled-sample precision is under about 0.8, stop and report untestable.
design.controls: Use a model with team and player fixed effects, opponent, lineup strength, score margin, period, shot-clock time at the PNR, season and regular season/playoff indicator, and the initiator's baseline PNR PPP estimated out-of-sample (shrinkage, to limit regression to the mean). Match or weight on elapsed possession time and drive characteristics, and report results with and without foul-ending possessions. Do not use matchup-based coverage fields (FAM:SF-APPS-058).
design.falsification: Placebo 1: assign a pseudo-drive timestamp (random prior action such as a pass) before PNRs and require a null. Placebo 2: shuffle drive labels within team-season. Placebo 3: check that the drive-to-PNR association appears under label rules unrelated to outcomes. Also test whether the drive effect is the same with the proxy-calibrated PNR labels and with raw PBP PNR labels. Divergence indicates a label artifact.
design.multiplicity: One pre-specified primary pooled test; secondary player-level heterogeneity analyses use false discovery rate control (Benjamini-Hochberg) with partial pooling, and only strata with sufficient n are reported.
design.decision_rule: Supported if the pooled effect is positive with a 95% cluster-robust CI above zero, passes placebos, is consistent across seasons, and replicates in the 2025-26 holdout. Rejected if the CI excludes effects above the minimum effect of interest. Artifact if the effect disappears under placebo, with foul-ending possessions removed, or under raw-PBP PNR labels. Untestable if label precision or exposure counts miss the pre-specified thresholds. Otherwise uncertain.
design.data_version: Freeze per-game NBA stats API files and the derived possession graph as of 2026-06-14 (hash and record count), covering 2022-23 to 2024-25 and the complete 2025-26 regular season; the 2025-26 playoffs enter only after completion on 2026-06-21, as holdout. Record the label backfill and proxy-calibration version.

methodological_questions: Can a drive immediately preceding a PNR be reliably identified from play-by-play data?
Does a preceding teammate drive causally raise PNR PPP or is it confounded by player, lineup and opponent quality?
How reliable are derived play-type labels and does outcome-derived labeling bias PPP estimates?
Is there sufficient sample size of drive-then-PNR sequences to detect an effect?
args.query: Does any teammate drive preceding a pick-and-roll raise PNR points per possession, given play-type labeling and data quality constraints in play-by-play derived possession records?

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Research question (as posed on 2026-06-14, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.
